extracted.intended_audience: Colonial American public and advocates of independence
extracted.subtask_description: A persuasive political pamphlet arguing for American independence and proposing basic principles and structures for a continental government. It addresses the reasons to separate from Great Britain and offers concrete suggestions for representative institutions and a Continental Charter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Republican virtue over monarchy
rubrics_metrics.description: The republican (not monarchical) part of the constitution is what Englishmen glory in; when republican virtue fails, slavery ensues — monarchy poisons the republic by engrossing the commons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monarchy concentrates business in the king and corrupts representative institutions; avoid concentrating civil and military business on a single monarch because it swallows up the power and virtue of popular assemblies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continental unity is essential
rubrics_metrics.description: The present contest is the affair of a continent and posterity are involved; now is the seed time of continental union, faith and honor — the least fracture will widen with time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the struggle as continental in scope; protect the union now because small breaks will grow into larger, lasting wounds for posterity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arms decided the contest — reconciliation is closed
rubrics_metrics.description: By referring the matter from argument to arms, a new era is struck; whatever plans prior to the commencement of hostilities are superseded and useless — the appeal was the king's choice and the continent accepted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that debate has ended; continuing to treat pre-hostility proposals as relevant is fallacious. Policy and sentiments must reflect the new reality created by armed conflict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject reconciliation — it yields no true advantage
rubrics_metrics.description: No single advantage can be shown that the continent derives from connection with Great Britain; reconciliation tends to involve us in European quarrels and to make us a make-weight in British politics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate alleged benefits skeptically; economic and security arguments in favor of remaining tied to Britain are illusory because Britain's motive is interest, not attachment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid dependence that drags into European wars
rubrics_metrics.description: Any submission or dependence on Great Britain tends to involve this continent in European wars and quarrels and sets us at variance with nations who would otherwise seek our friendship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For national interest, steer clear of partial connections with European powers; independence preserves neutrality and trade relations with all Europe.

rubrics_metrics.name: America's economic viability independent of Britain
rubrics_metrics.description: American commerce (corn, imports/exports) will find markets in Europe and the continent's barrenness of gold and silver protects it from invaders; America would have flourished without European control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Economic self-sufficiency and trade as a basis for independence: do not overvalue Britain's role in American prosperity when considering political dependence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distant government is impractical
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not in the power of Britain to govern the continent with convenience or knowledge; running petitions thousands of miles is folly — a continent cannot be perpetually governed by an island.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer local/regional governance where practical business and lawmaking can be done promptly; logistical delays of distant rule make self-government necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence enables lawful self-legislation
rubrics_metrics.description: Independence means whether we shall make our own laws, or whether the king shall forbid laws he dislikes; being able to make our own laws is the core meaning of independency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess political arrangements by whether they permit the community to legislate freely for its own needs rather than subjecting laws to a remote negative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reconciliation risks temporary guardianship and instability
rubrics_metrics.description: Even the best terms from Britain can amount only to a temporary expedient or guardianship that lasts until the colonies 'come of age' — this interim will be unsettled, discouraging emigrants and prompting departures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid solutions that produce only temporary political fixes; they may inhibit growth, cause capital flight, and increase long-term instability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence as means to prevent civil war
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing but independency — a continental form of government — can keep the peace of the continent and preserve it inviolate from civil wars; a patched-up connexion is more likely to produce revolt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure government continentally and inclusively to obviate provincial jealousies and the conditions that lead to domestic insurrection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Annual assemblies with single president and domestic focus
rubrics_metrics.description: Let the assemblies be annual, with a President only. Representation more equal. Their business wholly domestic, and subject to the authority of a Continental Congress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor frequent, regular assemblies led by a single executive figure for deliberation; confine assemblies to domestic matters while coordinating continental affairs through Congress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equalized representation via districting and delegate quotas
rubrics_metrics.description: Divide each colony into six, eight, or ten convenient districts, each to send delegates so each colony sends at least thirty; the whole Congress to number at least 390.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use internal districting to equalize representation among colonies; ensure minimum delegation sizes to balance provincial influence in continental legislature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rotation and selection method for Congress president
rubrics_metrics.description: When delegates meet, take a colony by lot and let Congress choose (by ballot) a president from that colony's delegates; omit that colony in the next Congress's lot until all thirteen have rotated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ randomized rotation of colonies as the source pool for the presidency, combined with delegate balloting, to prevent permanent dominance by any one province.

rubrics_metrics.name: High threshold for laws — three-fifths majority
rubrics_metrics.description: In order that nothing may pass into a law but what is satisfactorily just, not less than three fifths of the Congress to be called a majority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set supermajority requirements (3/5) on legislation to ensure wide consensus and prevent narrow majorities from imposing unjust measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continental Conference to draft a Charter
rubrics_metrics.description: Hold a Continental Conference consisting of a committee of twenty-six members of Congress (two per colony), two members from each House of Assembly or Provincial Convention, and five representatives of the people at large chosen in the provincial capital(s), to frame a Continental Charter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine experienced national actors (Congress/Assemblies) with popularly chosen delegates to craft a foundational charter that balances knowledge and popular authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Charter content: structure, jurisdictions, and rights
rubrics_metrics.description: The Continental Charter should fix number and manner of choosing members of Congress/Assembly, dates of sitting, delineate business and jurisdiction between them, secure freedom and property to all men, and above all the free exercise of religion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the charter explicitly defines institutional arrangements, separation of authorities, and fundamental rights (property, conscience/religion) as a basis for legitimate government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law as sovereign (the law is king)
rubrics_metrics.description: In America the law is king; in free countries the law ought to be King, and there ought to be no other. Let the charter be proclaimed on the divine law; place a crown as symbol of law then demolish it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Symbolically and constitutionally elevate the rule of law above personified monarchy; remove monarchical symbols to emphasize legal sovereignty and distribute any residual symbols among the people.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form constitution now to prevent demagogues
rubrics_metrics.description: It is infinitely wiser and safer to form a constitution of our own in a cool deliberate manner while we have the power, than to trust such an event to time and chance—omission risks some Massanello arising to sweep away liberties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Act proactively to establish stable institutions; delaying constitution-making invites opportunists and violent usurpation of power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political design: maximize individual happiness with minimal national expense
rubrics_metrics.description: The science of the politician consists in fixing the true point of happiness and freedom; those who discover a mode of government that contains the greatest sum of individual happiness, with the least national expense, deserve gratitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate governmental proposals by their balance of personal liberty and public cost—seek systems that optimize welfare while minimizing burdens on the nation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence is feasible given current military strength
rubrics_metrics.description: The Continent hath, at this time, the largest body of armed and disciplined men of any power under Heaven; unity, not mere numbers, is the source of strength.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess claims about feasibility of independence by considering unified military readiness and discipline; unity among colonies amplifies defensive capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't trust Britain's interest-based protection
rubrics_metrics.description: Britain 'protected' the continent from motive of interest (trade/domination), not attachment; she defended the continent at our expense and would have defended other regions for the same motive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating historical 'protections' or offered safeguards, identify underlying motives (commercial/political self-interest) rather than assuming benevolent guardianship.
